name: Carlos Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Pruitt's, a garage on the old quarry road at the edge of town. Most of our work is vans and pickups for builders, plumbers and a couple of farms, so it's a lot of diesel servicing, suspension and the odd gearbox. Gary Pruitt runs it, and there's me, an older mechanic called Walt and an apprentice, Kieran. We open at half seven because the tradesmen want their vans back before lunch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the customers are working people who need their van to earn, so you matter to them. What wears me out is the rush, five vans all due back by noon and one of them with a seized bolt. I rent a little terraced house on my own, about a mile from my parents, and I've got around three months of money saved. Sometimes I ask the AI on my phone for a torque setting or a wiring colour, but mostly I ask Walt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said all along: a lot of noise from people selling stuff. At the garage I'd tell Gary we were right not to spend money on fancy software. Online I don't post much, maybe a thumbs up on somebody's joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means nothing much changes, and that suits me. The builders still need their vans, and a van still needs a mechanic. My own worry is just getting a deposit together for a house before prices go up again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Pruitt's and maybe ask Gary for more of the gearbox work, since that pays better. I'd keep putting 250 a month into savings for a deposit. And if the AI on my phone keeps getting the torque figures right, I'd use it a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's a decent life with a clear next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad drove buses for thirty years, and he'd say he heard the same about every new gadget. I'd agree with him and we'd go back to watching the football. He'd ask about the house, that's what he always asks about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that world that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary's getting older and he's not great with money, and I sometimes wonder if Pruitt's will keep going. But there are other garages nearby, so I'm not losing sleep. If it shut, I'd be working somewhere else within a month.

say: AI was a lot of **noise** from people selling stuff.
Gary was right not to spend money on **fancy software**.
think: Builders still need their vans, so **nothing much changes** for him.
His real worry is a **house deposit** before prices rise again.
do: Ask Gary for more **gearbox work**, which pays better.
Keep putting **250 a month** toward a house deposit.
Use the phone AI a bit more for **torque figures** if it stays reliable.
feel: **Calm**, with a decent life and a clear next step.
S0.quote: My dad drove buses for thirty years, and he'd say he heard the same about every new gadget.
fieldNote: His customers are **tradespeople** whose vans earn their living, which gives him pride.
His only pressure is a **house deposit**, and Gary's shaky bookkeeping.
He's confident he'd find **another garage** within a month if needed.

steps.text: Take on more gearbox jobs at Pruitt's garage
Save 250 a month toward a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a tool like any other, and the good ones will win out. At the garage I'd say let's see what works for the other places first before Gary spends a penny. Online I'd stay quiet, there's enough arguing already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the front of the business changes more than the back. The van fleets will get AI that books their services and orders parts, and quotes will be done by software. My hands are still needed for now, but Gary might not replace Walt when he retires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait about six months and watch what the garage on the bypass does with its new system. If it works, I'd learn the booking and parts software properly, maybe on a short evening course. And I'd keep saving the 250 a month, maybe push it to 300.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. My own job feels safe, but I can see the shop getting smaller around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Pruitt's would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kieran, the apprentice. He's eighteen and he's learning the old way, the way I did, and he might not get the hours. I'd tell him to learn the software early, even though I'm not rushing myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell Kieran to learn it early, but you'd wait six months. Isn't that a bit odd?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I've got the years in, he hasn't. If I'm wrong about waiting, I lose six months. If Kieran (the apprentice) waits, he might never get a full-time start.

say: AI is **a tool** like any other, and the good ones will win.
Let other garages **try it first** before Gary spends a penny.
think: The **front of the business** changes more than the workshop.
Gary might **not replace Walt** when he retires.
do: Watch the **bypass garage's** new system for six months first.
Learn the **booking and parts software** on a short evening course if it works.
Push savings from 250 to **300 a month**.
feel: **Uneasy**, feeling safe himself but watching the shop shrink around him.
S1.quote: If I'm wrong about waiting, I lose six months. If Kieran (the apprentice) waits, he might never get a full-time start.
fieldNote: He'd wait for **proof** from another garage before changing anything.
He holds the apprentice to a **different standard** than himself, and explains why.
He expects **fewer mechanics**, not his own job gone.

steps.text: Watch the bypass garage's new system for six months
Take an evening course on booking and parts software
Raise house savings to 300 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we got blindsided and the people at the top should have been ready. To the builders who come in I'd say keep your old vans running, they'll be worth something. Online I'd probably say it's every family for itself now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm out of a job by 2031, maybe earlier. Once AGI handles the booking and diagnosis in 2028, the fleets go to big depots, and Gary's little garage on the quarry road can't compete. I'd be 32 with no house and the trade I learned going away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give up on the house for now and move back in with my parents to save the rent, maybe 600 a month. I'd ask about work at the quarry, fixing the big diggers and haul trucks, because I reckon that heavy kit gets robots last. And I'd cancel anything I don't need, the car finance on my pickup first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Like I did everything right and the ground moved anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would moving back home feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Embarrassing, at 28. My mum would be pleased, my dad would say nothing and then fix up the back room. I'd pay them rent anyway, because I'm not taking charity, even from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the three-year gap before robots change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's three years of wages I'd squeeze every penny out of. If the thinking side goes in 2028, I'm still useful with a spanner until 2031. Three years is my window to get into heavy plant. I'd want to get there before everyone else tries.

say: We got **blindsided**, and the people at the top should have been ready.
Builders should **keep old vans running**, because they'll be worth something.
think: He expects to be out of a job by **2031**, maybe earlier.
Fleets would go to **big depots**, and Pruitt's couldn't compete.
do: Move back to his **parents' house** to save around 600 a month in rent.
Ask about fixing diggers and **haul trucks** at the quarry.
Cancel the **car finance** on his pickup first.
feel: **Gutted**, having done everything right only for the ground to move anyway.
S2.quote: If the thinking side goes in 2028, I'm still useful with a spanner until 2031. Three years is my window to get into heavy plant.
fieldNote: He treats the **three-year robot gap** as a window to switch to heavy machinery.
Moving home is **embarrassing** to him, so he'd insist on paying rent.
He blames **people at the top**, not the technology itself.

steps.text: Move back in with his parents and pay them rent
Apply to service diggers and haul trucks at the quarry
Cancel the car finance on his pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people stop arguing and get on with it. At the garage I'd tell Walt and Kieran to start thinking about what comes next. With my mates at the football club I'd say there's still work, just different work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is just enough to change lanes once, not twice. The thinking work goes in 2031 and the hands-on stuff in 2034, so I'd have time to finish a course. I'd be 35 when the robots come, which isn't too old to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give it a year to see which way things go, still at Pruitt's and saving 300 a month. Then I'd do the heavy vehicle technician course, two years of day release, to work on lorries and plant. I'd keep renting rather than buy, so I can move for work if I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's the kind I can live with. I've got a plan, I just don't love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a year before starting the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen lads rush into courses that went nowhere. I'd want to see who's hiring heavy vehicle mechanics in 2027 before I spend two years on it. If it's still in demand, I'll go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep renting. What does that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house, really. My parents bought a house at 26 and I'd hoped to do the same. Keeping my options open means I'm 30-odd and still renting. That sits wrong with me.

say: Five years is **enough time** if people stop arguing and get on with it.
think: Five years is enough to **change lanes once**, not twice.
At **35** when robots come, he's not too old to start again.
do: Wait **a year** at Pruitt's, saving 300 a month.
Do a two-year **heavy vehicle technician** course on day release.
Keep **renting** rather than buying, so he can move for work.
feel: **Anxious** but livable, with a plan he doesn't love.
S3.quote: My parents bought a house at 26 and I'd hoped to do the same. Keeping my options open means I'm 30-odd and still renting.
fieldNote: He'd **test the market** for a year before committing to a course.
Giving up the **house** hurts him more than changing jobs.
He's still **on the hook** for losing his current work, but has a route.

steps.text: Stay at Pruitt's for a year and watch who's hiring
Take the two-year heavy vehicle technician course
Keep renting instead of buying a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and any decent mechanic will find his way. At the garage I'd say the van work will be here for years yet. Online I'd say nothing, I'd just get on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years gives me most of a career in the trade. I could buy a house, pay a good chunk off, and still have time to switch. Robots don't reach the workshop till about 2039, when I'm 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a small house in the next two years with the deposit I've saved. I'd start using the AI more at work once Gary and Walt are using it too, for diagnostics and parts. And around 2033 I'd look at what the robot-repair work looks like and decide then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a small worry in the back. Like a bill you know is coming but not soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you plan for a family, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to settle down, find someone at church or through mates, have kids by my early thirties. With ten years, that feels possible. With two, I wouldn't even think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kieran (the apprentice) in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn both the spanners and the screens, and keep his eyes open. Ten years is long enough to get good and then switch. A young lad with a trade and a bit of sense will be fine.

say: Ten years is long, and **any decent mechanic** will find his way.
The **van work** will be here for years yet.
think: Robots arrive around **2039**, when he'd be 40.
He could **buy a house** and still switch work later.
do: Buy a **small house** in the next two years with his deposit.
Use AI for **diagnostics and parts** once Gary and Walt do.
Look at **robot-repair work** around 2033 and decide then.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a worry like a bill that's coming but not soon.
S4.quote: Ten years gives me most of a career in the trade. I could buy a house, pay a good chunk off, and still have time to switch.
fieldNote: The **decade** lets him do the house and family plans he gave up in faster pictures.
He'd still adopt AI only **once colleagues do**, true to form.
He sees his own work going eventually, but **not soon**.

steps.text: Buy a small house within two years
Use AI for diagnostics once Gary and Walt do
Revisit robot-repair work around 2033 before deciding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be back in my old bedroom at 28 with the trade going away and no time to learn another. What would help is the quarries and big depots taking on mechanics to train on heavy plant, paid while they learn, not a benefit cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the customers. If the builders and plumbers lose work too, nobody's paying for van repairs anyway. A garage is only as healthy as the people who drive in.

headlineQuote: A garage is only as healthy as the people who drive in.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old mechanic** at a van and pickup garage serving builders and farms.
He's **single**, renting near his parents and saving for a **house deposit**.
He takes up AI **only once proven**, preferring to ask an older colleague.
In the fast AGI picture he'd **move home** and chase heavy plant work at the quarry.
With **ten years** he'd buy a house and start a family first.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, back in his old bedroom with his trade going and no time to learn another.
whatWouldHelp: Quarries and depots **training mechanics** on heavy plant, paid while they learn.
Work, **not benefit cheques**, so people keep their pride.
